summary: Defines the security architecture for WebRTC, the protocol suite for real-time applications deployed in browsers.

plainLanguage.summary: A browser call has to be secure even though the website arranging the call sits in the middle. This RFC sets out how: the two browsers encrypt the call directly, check that they can reach each other, and can use an identity service to confirm who is on the other end.

questions: what is the webrtc security architecture

subtitle: How a browser call is kept private, and who is trusted to say who is calling.

tldr.problem: A WebRTC call runs between two browsers with a web server in the middle arranging it, so the server could in principle listen in or pretend to be the other party.
tldr.mechanism: The media is protected with DTLS-SRTP, the two browsers check reachability with ICE before any media flows, and an optional identity service can vouch for who the other caller is without involving the calling site.
tldr.outcome: Media is encrypted end to end between the browsers, the calling site cannot read it, and the browser is the root of trust: any security property the user wants must ultimately be guaranteed by the browser.

today: RFC 8827 is a Proposed Standard published in January 2021 and has not been obsoleted or updated. It is the architecture companion to RFC 8826; the RFC itself says its IdP-based peer authentication has not been widely adopted or implemented.

sections.title: What WebRTC Changes About Web Security
sections.content:
The Real-Time Communications on the Web Working Group standardized protocols for real-time communications between web browsers, generally called WebRTC. The major uses are real-time audio and video calls, web conferencing, and direct data transfer. Unlike most conventional real-time systems, such as SIP-based soft phones, WebRTC communications are directly controlled by a web server through a JavaScript API.

A simple system has one web server and two browsers. The server talks to each browser over HTTP, and the browsers talk to each other directly for the media. A more complicated system allows calls between domains, where the protocol used between the domains is not standardized by WebRTC but, given the installed base and the form of the WebRTC API, is likely to be something SDP-based like SIP, or something like XMPP.

This arrangement presents new security challenges, which are analyzed in a companion document. This document describes the security architecture that addresses those threats and requirements.
sections.plainLanguage: The website arranges the call but does not carry it. The audio and video go straight from one browser to the other, which changes what has to be protected.

sections.title: The Trust Model
sections.content:
The basic assumption is that network resources exist in a hierarchy of trust rooted in the browser, which serves as the user's Trusted Computing Base. Any security property the user wants enforced must ultimately be guaranteed by the browser, or transitively by a property the browser verifies. If the browser is compromised, no security guarantee is possible. There are cases such as internet kiosks where the user cannot really trust the browser that much, and the security provided is then limited by how much they trust it.

Optimally nothing outside the browser would have to be trusted, which is not possible for a working system. Other network elements fall into two classes: those the browser can authenticate, which can be granted permission to reach sensitive resources, and those it cannot, which are untrusted.

There are two major classes of authenticated entity. Calling services are web sites whose origin can be verified, optimally over HTTPS, though in some cases because the browser is on a topologically restricted network and can infer authentication from firewall behaviour. Other users are WebRTC peers whose origin can be verified cryptographically, optimally with DTLS-SRTP.

Being authenticated does not make an entity trusted. Just because a site can be verified does not mean the user should trust it with the camera and microphone, but it gives the user the chance to decide. The point of identification comes first, then the question of how much to trust.

Beyond these two classes, other network elements cannot generally be identified, so they cannot be trusted. That does not rule out interacting with them, but it means assuming they will behave maliciously and designing the system to be safe even then.
sections.plainLanguage: The browser is the only thing that has to be trusted. Everything else is either something the browser can check the identity of, or something to be treated as hostile until proven otherwise.

sections.title: How a Call Is Set Up
sections.content:
Alice is logged into a calling service and clicks a Call button, which instantiates a PeerConnection object. This needs no security check, since JavaScript from any origin is allowed to get that far. The service's code then creates a media stream with an audio track and a video track, and the first security check happens here: untrusted origins are not allowed to reach the camera and microphone, so the browser asks Alice for permission.

The browser generates a signaling message containing the media channel information, the ICE candidates, and a fingerprint attribute that binds the communication to a key pair. The key may simply be generated for that call or be specific to the site. Before sending the message, the PeerConnection code contacts the identity service and obtains an assertion binding Alice's identity to her fingerprint; the easiest way to think of it is as an OAuth token. The message goes to the signaling server over TLS, and the server passes a signaling message on to Bob's browser, which alerts Bob to the incoming call and to Alice's identity. Because Alice provided an assertion, Bob's browser contacts Alice's identity provider to verify it, which lets it show a trusted element in the browser chrome saying the call is from Alice.

Bob agrees, a PeerConnection is instantiated, Bob's browser asks him for device permission, and a return signaling message with media information, ICE candidates and a fingerprint goes back to Alice. At this point each side knows that the other wants a secure call. Based on the fingerprint in the message and that message having arrived securely, they know the signaling server claims the call is from Alice to Bob, and with an assertion they know that independently of the server.

Media consent verification is provided through ICE. Once those checks complete, Alice knows that Bob, or whoever the signaling service claims Bob is, is willing to exchange traffic with her, and that either Bob is at the address she verified with ICE or an attacker on the path to that address is detouring the traffic. An attacker who is on the path but not attached to the signaling service cannot spoof the checks, because they do not have the ICE credentials.

The two peers then set up secure channels with DTLS and DTLS-SRTP keying for SRTP on the media channel, and SCTP over DTLS for data channels. A DTLS handshake is performed on every component established by ICE, so with RTP and RTCP muxing and several media streams on one channel there is only one handshake. Once it completes, the keys are exported and used to key SRTP.

The one remaining property is consent freshness, so that Alice can check that Bob is still prepared to receive her traffic and does not keep sending large volumes to something that went abruptly offline. ICE specifies periodic STUN keepalives only when media is not flowing, so implementations are required to send keepalives using the consent freshness mechanism, and the session is terminated if a keepalive fails and no new ICE channels can be established.
sections.plainLanguage: The browser asks permission for the camera, sends a short description of the call including a fingerprint, and then the two browsers check that they can reach each other before any media flows. Only then do they set up the encryption.

sections.title: Web-Based Peer Authentication
sections.content:
The document records that the mechanism in this section was designed early in the process and that, in retrospect, the working group was too optimistic about the enthusiasm for it. At the time of publication it has not been widely adopted or implemented, and it appears here as a description of the state of the art.

The idea is that an endpoint can identify the other side directly, without trusting the signaling service. This matters for federated calls, and for calls on a site the user barely trusts, such as a poker site, to someone with an identity on a site they do trust. Web-based identity technologies such as OAuth or Facebook Connect all share a web-based identity provider that attests to the user's identity, which allows identity to be separated from calling: Alice could call you on a poker site but identify herself as alice@example.org.

The general principle is that the party being authenticated is the user and their browser, not the signaling site, and the relying party is the browser too. The browser must generate the input to the assertion process and display the result of verification in a way the calling site cannot imitate. The document does not require the browser to implement any particular identity protocol or support any particular provider; it provides a generic interface, so new providers and protocols can be introduced without changing the browser or the calling service.

Any federated identity protocol has three participants: the Authenticating Party, which is trying to establish its identity; the Identity Provider, which vouches for it; and the Relying Party, which tries to verify it. The browser learns which providers the user has an account with, either from user configuration or from the calling site.

There are two kinds of provider. An authoritative provider has verifiable control over some part of the identity space, such as the operator of a mail domain, and examples include DNSSEC, an identity system for SIP, and Facebook Connect. A third-party provider has no control over its part of the identity space but verifies users by some unspecified mechanism and then attests to it, as certificate authorities do for domain names. When an authoritative provider is used, the relying party need not explicitly trust it, because it can check that the provider really made the assertion. With a third-party provider the relying party must explicitly trust it, which means the browser needs a trust list, and for that reason the number of third-party providers has to be fairly small.

In operation, the PeerConnection component of the browser instantiates an IdP proxy, which loads the provider's JavaScript at a location determined by the provider's domain and runs it in the provider's security context. The proxy registers an object conforming to the API in the WebRTC specification, and the browser calls methods on it to create or verify identity assertions. The browser therefore knows only how to load the provider's JavaScript and how to call the generic assertion API.
sections.plainLanguage: An identity service can say that the person calling is a known user, without the website that arranged the call being involved. The browser talks to that service directly, in its own protected corner of the browser.

sections.title: The SDP Identity Attribute
sections.content:
The SDP identity attribute is a session-level attribute used by an endpoint to convey its identity assertion to its peer. The assertion value is encoded as base64. The procedures assume that the assertion is bound to the fingerprints of the endpoint; other ways of binding an assertion to the endpoint are outside the scope of this specification. The semantics of multiple identity attributes within an offer or answer are undefined, so implementations SHOULD include only one, and relying parties MAY ignore all but the first.

The identity-assertion value is a JSON encoded string containing two keys. assertion holds an opaque string consumed by the identity provider. idp holds a dictionary with one or two values identifying the provider.

An offerer that wants to give its assertion to the peer includes an identity attribute in the offer, along with one or more SDP fingerprint attributes, and the identity attribute MUST be bound to all the fingerprint attributes in the session description. An answerer may include or omit an identity attribute independently of what the offerer did. On receiving an offer or answer with an identity attribute, the answerer can use it to contact the identity provider and verify the peer's identity; if the verification fails, the answerer MUST discard the offer or answer as malformed.

When a session is modified, if the set of fingerprints is unchanged the sender MAY send the same identity attribute, and the established identity then applies to existing DTLS connections as well as new ones. If the fingerprints change, the sender MUST either send a new identity attribute or none at all, because the change also causes a new DTLS connection to be established, and the receiver MUST discard all previously established identities.
sections.plainLanguage: The identity claim travels in the session description, tied to the fingerprints of the keys the call will use. If the keys change, the old claim no longer applies and has to be thrown away.

sections.title: Device Permissions and User Consent
sections.content:
Implementations MUST obtain explicit user consent before giving access to the camera or microphone, and MUST at minimum support two permission models for HTTPS origins: requests for one-time camera and microphone access, and requests for permanent access. Because HTTP origins cannot be securely established against network attackers, implementations MUST refuse all permission grants for HTTP origins.

Implementations SHOULD also support requests for access that promise that media from the grant will be sent to a single communicating peer, such as Call customerservice@example.org, where the media stream is only routed through a connection that has been cryptographically verified, through the identity provider mechanism or an X.509 certificate in the DTLS-SRTP handshake, as being associated with the stated identity. The idea is that a user may have a narrow list of peers they are willing to talk to, and narrow grants let the browser enforce that.

The API MUST provide a mechanism for the requesting JavaScript to give up the ability to see or modify the media, and the user interface MUST clearly indicate when the camera and microphone are in use, must not be suppressible by the JavaScript, and must make it clear how to stop device access. If the indication would be hidden by minimizing the window or by an overlapping window, the browser SHOULD stop camera and microphone input when the indication is hidden.

Browsers MUST NOT allow permanent screen or application sharing permissions to be installed in response to a JavaScript request, requiring another user action such as a permission setting or an application install instead, and MUST provide a separate dialog for sharing permissions even if the media request is made at the same time. They must indicate any windows currently being shared unambiguously, and windows which are not visible MUST NOT be shared.

Browsers MAY permit the formation of data channels without direct user approval, since sites can always tunnel data through the server, so further restrictions add nothing. Implementations that support some form of direct user authentication SHOULD also let a user authorize calls only to specific peers, for example to a verified user or to any verified user in the address book, and SHOULD use a different user interface indication for calls in progress with directly verifiable identities.
sections.plainLanguage: The browser is the one that grants access to the camera and the microphone, and the site cannot quietly take it or hide that it is happening.

sections.title: IP Location Privacy
sections.content:
A side effect of the default ICE behaviour is that the peer learns the user's IP address, which leaks a lot of location information. The API requirements here are meant to mitigate that. They are not intended to protect the address from a malicious site, since a site learns at least a server-reflexive address from any HTTP transaction; they are meant to let a site cooperate with the user to hide the address from the other side of the call. Hiding the address from the server itself needs an explicit privacy-preserving mechanism on the client, such as the Tor Browser, and is out of scope.

The API MUST provide a mechanism for the JavaScript to suppress ICE negotiation, while perhaps still gathering candidates, until the user has decided to answer the call. That lets a user keep their address, and their online status, from a peer they do not answer. The API MUST also provide a mechanism for the calling application to indicate that only TURN candidates are to be used, which prevents the peer from learning the address at all, and that mechanism must also permit suppression of the related address field, since that leaks local addresses.

The API MUST further provide a mechanism to reconfigure an existing call to add non-TURN candidates. Together these allow negotiation to start immediately on an incoming call notification, which reduces delay, while still avoiding disclosure of the address until the user has decided to answer, and allow the address to be hidden for the whole call, or later revealed if the user no longer needs to hide it.

The security considerations add that these protections assume a non-malicious calling service. The calling service always knows the user's status and, absent something like Tor, their address, so it can violate the user's privacy at will; users who want privacy from the site need a separate privacy technology. Any identifier that persists across calls is a privacy problem, especially for anonymous calling services, which SHOULD instruct the browser to use separate DTLS keys for each call and to use TURN throughout the call, or the other side will learn linkable information that lets it correlate the browser across calls.
sections.plainLanguage: Setting up a call normally tells the other side your address. The browser has to offer the site a way to hold that back until the user agrees to talk.

sections.title: Communications Security
sections.content:
Implementations MUST support SRTP, MUST support DTLS and DTLS-SRTP for SRTP keying, and MUST support SCTP over DTLS. All media channels MUST be secured with SRTP and SRTCP, and media MUST NOT be sent over plain RTP or RTCP: implementations MUST NOT negotiate cipher suites with NULL encryption modes. DTLS-SRTP MUST be offered for every media channel, WebRTC implementations MUST NOT offer or select SDP security descriptions, and an SRTP Master Key Identifier MUST NOT be used. All data channels MUST be secured via DTLS.

All implementations MUST support DTLS 1.2 with the TLS_ECDHE_ECDSA_WITH_AES_128_GCM_SHA256 cipher suite and the P-256 curve. Earlier drafts of the specification required DTLS 1.0 with a different cipher suite, and some implementations do not support DTLS 1.2, so endpoints that support only DTLS 1.2 might meet interoperability problems. The DTLS-SRTP protection profile SRTP_AES128_CM_HMAC_SHA1_80 MUST be supported. Implementations MUST favour cipher suites that provide forward secrecy over ones that do not, and SHOULD favour authenticated encryption with associated data over the alternatives. Implementations MUST NOT implement DTLS renegotiation and MUST reject it with a no_renegotiation alert, and endpoints MUST NOT implement TLS False Start.

The API MUST generate a new authentication key pair for every new call by default, which allows unlinkability, and MUST provide a means to reuse a key pair for calls. Unless the user configures an external key pair, different key pairs MUST be used for each origin, which avoids creating a super-cookie. When DTLS-SRTP is used, the API MUST NOT permit the JavaScript to obtain the negotiated keying material, which preserves the end-to-end security of the media.

A user-oriented client MUST provide an inspector interface where the user can find the security characteristics of the media. The client MUST let a user determine the security characteristics of the displayed audio and video streams and of their own outgoing transmissions, and where the far end was directly verified, the characteristics MUST include the verified information. The characteristics MUST also indicate the cryptographic algorithms in use, whether forward secrecy is provided, and include a means of out-of-band verification such as a certificate fingerprint or a Short Authentication String.
sections.plainLanguage: Media is always encrypted, with a specific modern cipher suite, and the site cannot get at the keys. The user can also ask the browser what protection the call is using.

items.text: The root of trust. Every security guarantee must end up here.
